featured.reason: Caveman (Apache-2.0) is a token-saving skill, CLI and proxy for coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode and 30+ others: a short reply voice that leaves code, paths and errors verbatim, a “read less” compressor for logs/JSON/CSV/test output, Blocks (reuse scripts the agent writes), and optional Auto model routing. Official Claude Code plugin, Codex skills (`$caveman`), `npx skills add JuliusBrussee/caveman`, and a Gemini extension. Rated 4 rather than 5 because the full CLI installer auto-detects agents and logins and sends usage stats (commands, token counts, OS, IP) by default unless `caveman telemetry off` or `DO_NOT_TRACK=1`; Auto/Cloud can send prompts once signed in. The skill-only install does not need the proxy.
ideas: Install only the skill, not the full CLI (`npx skills add JuliusBrussee/caveman -g`), then type `/caveman` or `/ultracave` in Claude Code (`$caveman` in Codex) on the next ai-daily-radar change so replies stay short while code, paths and error text stay verbatim.

If you later try the CLI, run `caveman telemetry off` or set `DO_NOT_TRACK=1` first, and leave Auto/Cloud off so prompts, CLAUDE.md and tool results are not sent to Caveman Cloud; the default installer also detects existing agent logins.

Use the read-less compressor on bulky logs, JSON or test output from a site publish or the daily archive run, so Claude Code or Codex spend fewer input tokens on the same files (the README's session runs showed about a 33% cut, with HTML still a weak spot).
Turn on Blocks for a repeated chore such as a post-publish check script, so the agent reuses the script it already wrote instead of regenerating it each time.

Read the skill rules (answer first, one idea per sentence, never rewrite the user prompt, stop and use full sentences for security or irreversible steps) and copy that pattern when you package a shared skill such as CLI-Anything.

news_highlights.title: Lovable apps expose passport details and more than 200K private messages
news_highlights.why_it_matters: Hamburg researchers at Crissy Field (with Handelsblatt) reviewed 159,041 Lovable AI-generated apps and 34,545 that used Supabase. On 24,664 sites that already loaded database rows without a login, further read-only queries found email addresses in 10,560 tables across 7,403 apps. Concrete cases include a German forum exposing 80,000+ profiles and 200,000+ chat messages, plus 1,000+ identity-document records with passport numbers. Recurring Supabase patterns make the same access-control mistake easy to hunt at scale — a reminder that an AI app builder does not review permissions for you.

news_highlights.title: Chinese frontier AI models carry the fingerprint of export-controlled GPUs
news_highlights.why_it_matters: Will DePue at Unemployment Labs recovered initialization fingerprints from published weights: six models released since April 2026 by DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group match NVIDIA Blackwell layouts (148 SMs for B200/B300, or 152 for GB200/GB300), while earlier models from the same labs match Hopper. The match was reproduced on physical Blackwell chips for DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Kimi K3. The author is careful: this is evidence of access at initialization, not of where the chips sat, how they were obtained, or an export-control violation. Newer Qwen, GLM and several other Chinese labs still read as Hopper.

news_highlights.title: Advancing science and engineering with Antigravity's /teamwork
news_highlights.why_it_matters: Google Research describes Antigravity's /teamwork as a multi-agent harness on Gemini 4 that splits context across specialists and checks candidates with independent verifiers such as Lean 4 and unmodified test suites. Among the claimed results: a Lean formalization of the Weil conjectures (~1.8 million lines), a remaining Zircon C++ rewrite into about 800,000 lines of safe Rust that boots on arm64, and a Rust port of the libgav1 AV1 decoder that ended 20–30% faster than the original. /teamwork, /boost and Deep Review are available in Antigravity for external users.

news_highlights.title: Project Zero will disclose vulnerabilities 90 days after reporting
news_highlights.why_it_matters: On 13 Nov 2026 Project Zero replaced its 90+30 policy with “Full 90”: details go public 90 days after a report, with no 30-day patch soak. Natalie Silvanovich argues LLMs have sped up both discovery and patch-to-exploit, so soak time now mainly creates a false sense of secrecy, and some targets that used to yield a few bugs a year now yield several a week. The window tightens to 60 days on 2 Feb 2027 and 30 days on 3 Jan 2028, with exceptions only for in-the-wild exploits, already-public bugs, or a vendor request.

news_highlights.title: PyPI's redesigned project pages with clearer security signals are now live
news_highlights.why_it_matters: PyPI's new Security tab is live, showing whether a release has full, no, incomplete, inconsistent, changed, or lost provenance from digital attestations (Trusted Publisher and SLSA build provenance). Warnings also appear at the top of the project page. “No provenance” is common for older uploads and is not itself proof of malice, but a sudden loss or change of provenance is worth checking before you install — a practical supply-chain signal for everyday pip/uv use.
